name: CTEs & Problem Decomposition
goal: Break a vague, layered question into named steps a reviewer can follow — and compare rows against a benchmark you computed.

brief.from: Sana Kapoor · Head of Growth — sent 11:48 pm
brief.body: Quick one (sorry, late) — investors want to understand our customer base quality. Who are our best customers, how concentrated is revenue in them, and are good customers going quiet that we should win back? I don't need a dashboard, I need the logic. Something before the 10am sync? Real-world skill: 'best', 'quality', 'going quiet' are undefined — your first job is to define them in measurable terms and state your definitions.

clinic.title: CTEs as readable thinking
clinic.body: A WITH chain names each step — compute per-customer value → compute a benchmark → compare — so the query reads top-to-bottom like an argument. Prefer a CTE chain over deeply nested subqueries; reviewers (and future-you) can actually follow it.

classwork.title: LTV tiers & the Pareto question — together

steps.instr: One LTV value per customer (net of returns, off customers_clean).
steps.sql:
WITH cust_ltv AS (
  SELECT c.CustomerID,
    SUM(CASE WHEN o.ReturnFlag='Yes' THEN 0 ELSE o.Revenue END) AS ltv,
    COUNT(*) AS orders
  FROM customers_clean c JOIN orders o ON c.CustomerID = o.CustomerID
  GROUP BY c.CustomerID
)
SELECT * FROM cust_ltv ORDER BY ltv DESC LIMIT 10;
steps.checkpoint: LTV is net of returns, computed off customers_clean (no double-counting).

steps.instr: Bucket into tiers, then answer the concentration question.
steps.sql:
WITH cust_ltv AS (
  SELECT c.CustomerID,
    SUM(CASE WHEN o.ReturnFlag='Yes' THEN 0 ELSE o.Revenue END) AS ltv, COUNT(*) AS orders
  FROM customers_clean c JOIN orders o ON c.CustomerID = o.CustomerID GROUP BY c.CustomerID),
tiered AS (
  SELECT *, CASE WHEN ltv>=100000 THEN 'Platinum' WHEN ltv>=50000 THEN 'Gold' WHEN ltv>=20000 THEN 'Silver' ELSE 'Bronze' END AS tier
  FROM cust_ltv)
SELECT tier, COUNT(*) AS customers, ROUND(SUM(ltv),0) AS tier_revenue,
  ROUND(AVG(orders),1) AS avg_orders,
  ROUND(SUM(ltv)/(SELECT SUM(ltv) FROM tiered)*100,1) AS pct_of_total_revenue
FROM tiered GROUP BY tier ORDER BY tier_revenue DESC;
steps.checkpoint: Headline sentence, e.g. 'Platinum+Gold are ~18% of customers but ~61% of revenue.' Thresholds are business choices, not laws.

classwork.reference:
WITH cust_ltv AS (
  SELECT c.CustomerID,
    SUM(CASE WHEN o.ReturnFlag='Yes' THEN 0 ELSE o.Revenue END) AS ltv, COUNT(*) AS orders
  FROM customers_clean c JOIN orders o ON c.CustomerID = o.CustomerID GROUP BY c.CustomerID),
tiered AS (
  SELECT *, CASE WHEN ltv>=100000 THEN 'Platinum' WHEN ltv>=50000 THEN 'Gold' WHEN ltv>=20000 THEN 'Silver' ELSE 'Bronze' END AS tier FROM cust_ltv)
SELECT tier, COUNT(*) AS customers, ROUND(SUM(ltv),0) AS tier_revenue,
  ROUND(AVG(orders),1) AS avg_orders,
  ROUND(SUM(ltv)/(SELECT SUM(ltv) FROM tiered)*100,1) AS pct_of_total_revenue
FROM tiered GROUP BY tier ORDER BY tier_revenue DESC;

tickets.title: Customers who out-spend their own segment's average
tickets.prompt: Within each segment, find customers whose net lifetime spend exceeds that segment's average. Build it as a CTE chain off customers_clean. Output exactly four columns — Segment, CustomerID, net_spend (rounded 0), segment_avg (rounded 0) — one row per qualifying customer. Row order doesn't matter (graded as a set). net_spend = SUM of revenue with returns zeroed; segment_avg = the average of those per-customer net spends within the segment.
acceptanceCriteria: Each customer compared to their OWN segment average, not the global
Built as a CTE chain, using customers_clean
hints: CTE 1: per-customer net_spend grouped by CustomerID, Segment (from customers_clean).
Join and keep rows where net_spend > seg_avg.

tickets.title: "Rising star" products — beat category on revenue AND rating
tickets.prompt: Find products exceeding their category's average revenue AND median rating — candidates for the investor growth story. Two benchmarks computed per category, then compared.
acceptanceCriteria: Category average revenue AND median rating computed as benchmarks
hints: CTE 1: per-product revenue + Rating (join products to orders).
tickets.solution:
WITH prod AS (
  SELECT p.ProductID, p.ProductName, p.Category, p.Rating, ROUND(SUM(o.Revenue),0) AS revenue
  FROM products p JOIN orders o ON p.ProductID = o.ProductID
  GROUP BY p.ProductID, p.ProductName, p.Category, p.Rating),
cat_bench AS (
  SELECT Category, AVG(revenue) AS cat_avg_revenue, median(Rating) AS cat_median_rating
  FROM prod GROUP BY Category)
SELECT pr.Category, pr.ProductName, pr.revenue, pr.Rating,
  ROUND(cb.cat_avg_revenue,0) AS cat_avg_revenue, cb.cat_median_rating
FROM prod pr JOIN cat_bench cb ON pr.Category = cb.Category
WHERE pr.revenue > cb.cat_avg_revenue AND pr.Rating > cb.cat_median_rating
ORDER BY pr.Category, pr.revenue DESC;
tickets.modelNote: DuckDB uses median(Rating) or quantile_cont(Rating,0.5). On Databricks the same benchmark is percentile_approx(Rating,0.5).

tickets.title: Win-back list: high-value customers gone quiet
tickets.prompt: Answer Sana's 'good customers going quiet.' Define it, then build the list: customers with >=3 lifetime orders whose most recent order is >180 days before the latest date in the data. Rank by LTV. Defend your thresholds.
acceptanceCriteria: 'Quiet' defined relative to the dataset's max date, not today
Output ranked by net LTV with days-since-last-order
hints: DuckDB days-between: date_diff('day', last_order_date, data_max). (Spark: DATEDIFF(data_max, last_order_date).)
tickets.solution:
WITH per_cust AS (
  SELECT o.CustomerID, COUNT(*) AS lifetime_orders, MAX(o.OrderDate) AS last_order_date,
    SUM(CASE WHEN o.ReturnFlag='Yes' THEN 0 ELSE o.Revenue END) AS net_ltv
  FROM orders o GROUP BY o.CustomerID),
bound AS (SELECT MAX(OrderDate) AS data_max FROM orders)
SELECT pc.CustomerID, pc.lifetime_orders, pc.last_order_date,
  date_diff('day', pc.last_order_date, (SELECT data_max FROM bound)) AS days_since_last,
  ROUND(pc.net_ltv,0) AS net_ltv
FROM per_cust pc
WHERE pc.lifetime_orders >= 3
  AND date_diff('day', pc.last_order_date, (SELECT data_max FROM bound)) > 180
ORDER BY pc.net_ltv DESC;
tickets.modelNote: Threshold rationale example: '180 days ~ 2x our median repeat interval, so a gap that long signals real disengagement; the >=3-order floor restricts the list to customers with a relationship worth saving.' Note the DuckDB date_diff argument order (unit, start, end).
